title: Marking When a Cell Was Born
endLine: A DNA pulse marks when cells stopped dividing, not their identity.

scenes.tts: Every neuron here looks finished. Which ones were born first? An adult brain carries no date stamps on its cells. To learn when cells were born, biologists turn DNA copying itself into a clock.
scenes.caption: Every neuron here looks finished. Which ones were born first? An adult brain carries no date stamps on its cells. To learn when cells were born, biologists turn DNA copying itself into a clock.
scenes.visual: Schematic cross-section of adult brain tissue fills the frame height: a bottom ventricular zone with radial fibres rising through layered neurons that drift gently. All neurons look identical in neutral muted colour while a pulsing question appears above: 'Which ones were born first?'. As DNA copying is named, a luminous ring flashes briefly inside one bottom cell's nucleus to preview a clock.
scenes.narration: Every neuron here looks finished. Which ones were born first? An adult brain carries no date stamps on its cells. To learn when cells were born, biologists turn DNA copying itself into a clock.

scenes.visual: Same schematic brain cross-section continues subtle ambient drift; the title 'Marking When a Cell Was Born' fades cleanly over the upper tissue band and then clears.

scenes.tts: A dividing cell copies its DNA once per division, in S phase. A neuron that stopped dividing normally does not copy its genome again. Biologists give a brief pulse of a thymidine analog, a labelled DNA building block. Because thymidine goes only into DNA, every cell in S phase builds it in.

scenes.visual: Camera zooms smoothly onto the bottom ventricular zone of the same schematic tissue while a quiet mature neuron sits above it. Inside one dividing progenitor, schematic chromosome bars double during S phase; the mature neuron above stays still. A colour wash labelled 'Pulse' sweeps across the tissue as glowing dot markers (schematic, no molecular structures) enter only the S-phase nuclei and lock onto their chromosomes.
scenes.narration: A dividing cell copies its DNA once per division, in S phase. A neuron that stopped dividing normally does not copy its genome again. scenes.tts: Next comes the chase: the label is gone, and time moves on. A labelled progenitor that divides one last time passes heavy label to two daughters. Those newborn neurons never divide again, so they stay heavily labelled for life. Progenitors that keep dividing split that label roughly in half each division.

scenes.visual: A schematic timeline advances from 'Pulse' into 'Chase' as the background wash clears. Two brightly labelled progenitors sit side by side in the ventricular zone. On the left, one divides once into two brightly glowing daughters that climb upward into the tissue wall and keep full brightness. On the right, the second progenitor divides repeatedly; beside it, a schematic brightness bar cuts cleanly in half at each split as its daughters grow dimmer.

scenes.tts: Heavy label therefore marks an approximate last S phase, when the cell stopped dividing. In the cortical plate, earlier birthdays settle deeper, and younger ones sit higher. Early work used radioactive tritiated thymidine, followed later by B r d U. A newer mimic, E d U, is detected by click chemistry, which attaches a fluorescent tag.

scenes.visual: Camera pulls slightly back on the same schematic cortical wall. An early-pulse batch of heavily labelled neurons settles in a deep lower layer while a later-pulse batch in a second hue sits higher toward the top, with a 'Last S phase' tag beside the bright nuclei. Along a clean bottom strip, three simple colour-coded badge labels appear in sequence—tritiated thymidine, BrdU, and fluorescent EdU with a bright glow ring (all schematic, no molecular structures).

scenes.tts: Still, a glowing nucleus alone can mislead. Picture an injured tissue whose cells are thought to be non-dividing. After a pulse, a B r d U positive nucleus appears. Must that cell have passed through S phase?
scenes.caption: Still, a glowing nucleus alone can mislead. Picture an injured tissue whose cells are thought to be non-dividing. After a pulse, a BrdU-positive nucleus appears. Must that cell have passed through S phase?
scenes.visual: The same schematic tissue shifts to an injured adult patch marked by a subtle ragged gap, where surrounding cells sit still and quiet. A brief pulse washes across, and a single nucleus near the injury glows bright with a 'BrdU+' tag. The question appears clearly above: 'Must this cell have passed through S phase?'
scenes.narration: Still, a glowing nucleus alone can mislead. Picture an injured tissue whose cells are thought to be non-dividing. After a pulse, a BrdU-positive nucleus appears. Must that cell have passed through S phase?

scenes.visual: The injured schematic tissue holds steady with the glowing BrdU+ nucleus pulsing slowly beside a soft '?' marker, the question pinned above, and a smooth progress bar advancing across the bottom for the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: No. Repair also builds short new DNA stretches that analogs can enter. In injured tissue, B r d U alone cannot separate repair from replication without cell-cycle evidence. Nor is a birth record a cell identity. Under a light microscope, label might belong to a glial cell, a support cell, pressed against a neuron. Confirming cell type takes an extra check, like electron microscopy.

scenes.visual: Inside that same glowing nucleus, a schematic DNA strand shows a small patched break glowing with label, labelled 'DNA repair' beside a cross over 'S phase?', while a small badge calls for cell-cycle evidence. The view then pans gently to a neuron in the tissue wall with a labelled glial cell pressed tightly against it: a blurry 'Light microscope' halo merges them into one spot, then sharpens into an 'Electron microscopy' outline separating the labelled glial cell from the unlabelled neuron (all schematic).

scenes.tts: That check showed adult brains can make neurons. In the 1960s, Joseph Altman found labelled cells in rat dentate gyrus and moving toward the olfactory bulb. In 1977, Michael Kaplan and James Hinds used electron microscopy to confirm they were neurons. In 1983, Goldman and Nottebohm tracked new adult canary neurons from ventricle to song nucleus H V C.

scenes.visual: Returning to the carried schematic brain cross-section with a clean timeline along the bottom, three milestones animate in sequence: '1960s · Altman' lights up tritiated-thymidine cells in a schematic adult rat dentate gyrus and olfactory bulb path; '1977 · Kaplan & Hinds' places an electron-microscopy check over those neurons; '1983 · Goldman & Nottebohm' traces glowing adult canary cells born at the ventricular zone migrating outward along fibres into the song nucleus HVC.

scenes.tts: E d U can also separate division speed from daughter fate. A short pulse roughly measures rate; a chase shows what labelled daughters become. In 2023, Abby and colleagues tracked mouse clones lacking one or both copies of Notch one. The clones expanded without dividing faster. E d U tracking fit more daughters staying progenitors: fate, not speed.

scenes.visual: The bottom dividing layer transitions smoothly into a schematic basal tissue strip with a two-part timeline: 'Short EdU pulse' versus 'Chase'. A small caution tag beside the pulse readout: 'also depends on S-phase length and cycling cells'. In a '2023 · Abby & colleagues' schematic clone lacking one or both Notch1 copies, which grows as large as or larger than control without a higher pulse labelling, pulse labelling stays similar to control, while after the chase more brightly labelled daughters remain as basal progenitors and fewer differentiate upward—labelled 'Fate, not speed'.

scenes.tts: Across tissues, the rule holds. Pair a timed DNA pulse with controls, and heavy label records a last division. What the cell became still needs its own proof.
scenes.caption: Across tissues, the rule holds. Pair a timed DNA pulse with controls, and heavy label records a last division. What the cell became still needs its own proof.
scenes.visual: The view zooms back out to the full schematic brain cross-section with bright birthdated neurons resting calmly in their layers, a small 'Last division' bracket on the pulse timeline and a separate 'Identity check' checkmark beside a confirmed neuron.
scenes.narration: Across tissues, the rule holds. Pair a timed DNA pulse with controls, and heavy label records a last division. What the cell became still needs its own proof.

scenes.visual: The schematic tissue dims softly behind a few gently drifting labelled nuclei as the end line settles cleanly in large bright text: 'A DNA pulse marks when cells stopped dividing, not their identity.'
